A priest and aristocrat who commanded the rebels in Galilee, surrendered at Jotapata in 67, predicted Vespasian's rise, and watched the siege from Titus' staff. His Jewish War is our main source, written in Rome under Flavian patronage, and every page reflects both his eyewitness knowledge and his need to justify himself.

A veteran commander from a modest family whom Nero sent to crush the revolt in 67. He subdued Galilee and much of Judea, was proclaimed emperor by the eastern legions in July 69, and founded the Flavian dynasty. The victory over Judea became a central piece of his regime's propaganda.
Roman commander at the siege, emperor 79-81

Vespasian's elder son, who took command in 70 and captured Jerusalem after about five months, with the former prefect of Egypt Tiberius Julius Alexander as his chief of staff. Josephus portrays him as brave and merciful and insists he wanted to save the temple; other ancient evidence and many modern historians are more sceptical. His arch still stands in the Roman Forum.

Marched on Jerusalem in autumn 66 to put down the revolt, burned Bezetha and attacked the temple's north wall, then withdrew unexpectedly and was routed in the Beth-horon pass. The defeat emboldened the rebels and made a full Roman war inevitable. He died soon after, perhaps in 67.

Josephus paints him as a greedy and provocative governor who all but wanted a revolt to cover his crimes. His seizure of temple funds and the massacre that followed in 66 lit the fuse of the war. Even Tacitus says Jewish patience lasted until Florus.

A Galilean leader and Josephus' bitter rival, who escaped to Jerusalem in 67, allied with the Zealots and eventually controlled the temple area. Josephus calls him a tyrant and blames him for sacrilege. Captured starving in the tunnels under the city, he was sentenced to life imprisonment.
Rebel leader holding the upper and lower city

A charismatic commander who freed slaves and gathered a large army in the countryside, and was invited into Jerusalem in 69 to counter John. He held most of the city during the siege. He surrendered after the fall, was paraded in the triumph in Rome, and executed in the Forum as the enemy general.
Zealot leader in the inner temple

A priest who led the Zealots and broke from John to hold the inner courts of the temple, living on the sacred stores. At Passover 70 John's men infiltrated the temple and absorbed his faction, leaving two parties in the city instead of three.
Jewish king and his sister, allies of Rome

The last of the Herodian royal family. In 66 they urged the people not to go to war, and Agrippa's speech in Josephus is a long plea that Rome could not be beaten. They then sided with Rome, and Berenice became Titus' lover, though Roman opinion prevented their marriage.

A countryman who, from the Feast of Tabernacles in 62, cried 'Woe to Jerusalem' through the streets for over seven years. Flogged by the Jewish leaders and the Roman governor Albinus, he never defended himself, and he was killed by a Roman stone during the siege. His story is often compared with the trial of Jesus of Nazareth.
Former high priest and moderate leader

The high priest who had James, the brother of Jesus, executed in 62 according to Josephus' Antiquities, and who later led the provisional government in Jerusalem. Josephus admired him as a realist who hoped to make terms with Rome. He was killed by the Zealots and Idumeans in the winter of 67-68.
Leader of the Sicarii at Masada

A relative of the earlier rebel Judas the Galilean, he led the Sicarii, the 'dagger men', who held Masada from 66. In Josephus' account he persuaded the defenders to die rather than be enslaved. The speeches Josephus gives him are literary compositions.

Almost certainly inflated. Josephus explains the total by the Passover crowds trapped in the city, but modern estimates of Jerusalem's population, even swollen by refugees, run from tens of thousands to a few hundred thousand. Tacitus gives 600,000 besieged.
A more plausible order of magnitude, possibly drawn from Roman records. Captives were sent to the Egyptian mines, the arenas of the provinces, or sold as slaves.

Josephus says the priests counted 256,500 Passover lambs and multiplied by ten diners each. The figure is far beyond what Jerusalem and its surroundings could hold and is not taken literally by historians, though it shows how large the pilgrim festivals were.

A plausible length for a circuit around the city's hills, though building it in three days, even with the whole army, is remarkable. Little or nothing of it has been securely identified on the ground.

From Titus' arrival around Passover (Xanthicus, about April) to the fall of the upper city on 8 Gorpieus (about September) AD 70. The exact Roman equivalents of Josephus' Macedonian month names are debated.

Josephus includes women and children in this total. Excavations found only a few dozen skeletons, which may reflect later disturbance, Roman disposal of bodies or exaggeration; the figure cannot be confirmed.
